title: As a hen (Matthew 23:13–39)
hook: woe after woe, like a call-out thread, and then the last picture is a hen
carry: how often I would have gathered you
tomorrow: the buildings are huge. what does he say about them?

segments.voice: One teacher, everyone else brethren, and a word for servant that became the word for deacon: the greatest serves. The same chapter now gets loud.

A call-out thread has a rhythm: a name, a charge, a screenshot, again and again. The second half of Matthew 23 has that drumbeat. "Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites!" Then again. Blind guides. Whited sepulchres, white on the outside, full of bones within. It reads like thunder. And then, at the very end, the voice changes, and the last picture Jesus uses for himself is not a judge, not a lion, not a storm. It's a hen. Why end the fire with a farm bird?
screen: `A CALL-OUT THREAD.` → `WOE UNTO YOU.` → `THEN, A HEN?`

segments.voice: Start with what the woes are about. "Ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone." He doesn't mock the small herbs. Do those, he says, and don't drop the heavy things. The target is a gap between the polished outside and the center. And these are words from a Jewish teacher to the holy city of his own people, in the old voice of Israel's prophets, who also cried woe. Now the turn. "O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!" There's the answer to the puzzle. The fire was never the opposite of love. It was what love sounds like when it watches people it cares about get hurt. A hen doesn't win fights. She spreads her wings between the chicks and whatever is coming, and stays. The Psalms know that shelter: "under his wings shalt thou trust." Notice the last words too: ye would not. The wings open; nobody is dragged under. And the chapter ends with a door left open: you won't see me, he says, until you say, "Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord."
screen: `WEIGHTIER MATTERS: JUDGMENT, MERCY, FAITH.` · `A JEWISH TEACHER TO HIS OWN CITY.` · `AS A HEN GATHERETH HER CHICKENS.` · `AND YE WOULD NOT.` · then, large: `HOW OFTEN I WOULD HAVE GATHERED YOU.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who has made you angry lately, someone you still care about. Open your arms wide, like wings, and feel the heat of it for a breath. Then let your arms slowly fold in, as if gathering, and look underneath the anger for what you want for them.
As a hen. The picture Jesus chooses at the end of the woes: a mother bird gathering her chicks under her wings.
Your line: how often I would have gathered you. Even the woes end with open wings. Back tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Christian prayers and paintings picture Christ as a mother hen gathering her chicks, drawing on this verse, and some churches read Matthew 23 as a mirror for their own leaders first.

notes: Sensitive passage: the woes have been used against Jews. The voice frames them as words from a Jewish teacher to the holy city of his own people, in the manner of Israel's prophets, centers the critique on the gap between surface and center, and a myth item corrects the popular misreading. Please check carefully.
'Ye pay tithe' is quoted with a capital in the voice; 23:23 KJV reads 'for ye pay tithe'. Confirm.
'Whited sepulchres, white on the outside, full of bones within' paraphrases 23:27 ('full of dead men's bones'). Confirm.
'In the old voice of Israel's prophets, who also cried woe' rests on Isaiah 5:8–22 (a series of woes); confirm the framing.
